learnings.adapt_needed: Tie any state support to EPS to efficiency and bill-collection targets and a closure timeline for the oldest units.
learnings.blockers: Keeping end-user prices low is a political priority, so utility losses and state support are likely to persist.
learnings.quote: The fiscal support subsidies for electricity generation from coal in Kosovo* were related to the government loan to cover the cost of KEK's regular operating activities caused by the low operational efficiency of the TPP and problems with the collection of electricity bills, in the amount the EUR 4,79 million and EUR 5,53 million in 2021 and 2022 respectively (see Annex 2).

learnings.title: Serbia leads Electricity Integration Package transposition, but coupling still not reached
learnings.programme: Energy Community Electricity Integration Package (market coupling)
learnings.problem: Until its market is coupled with the EU day-ahead and intraday markets, Serbia cannot qualify for the CBAM exemption for electricity.
learnings.solution: Serbia adopted a comprehensive set of primary and secondary acts to fully transpose the Electricity Integration Package, the legal basis for joining EU market coupling. The Secretariat and the European Commission must then verify compliance.
learnings.funding: The EU Reform and Growth Facility for the Western Balkans ties its support to binding deadlines for adopting this legislation.
learnings.results: As of 9 September 2025 Serbia had day-ahead and intraday markets running and its transposition framework adopted, but compliance was not yet verified. No Contracting Party met the 31 December 2023 deadline and none is expected to join EU market coupling before 2027, so CBAM applies from 1 January 2026.
learnings.serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own path to the CBAM exemption: it is closest to the 'point of no return', but after that the pace depends on EU bodies. Growth Facility deadlines add EU funding conditionality to the legal obligation.
learnings.adapt_needed: Serbia needs to submit complete laws with good-quality English concordance tables quickly, so that the Secretariat and Commission verification and the 18-month technical preparation can start.
learnings.blockers: Verification of the transposition, approval of the market coupling integration plan by ACER and the stalled Shadow SEE capacity calculation region, held up by the Serbia–Kosovo dispute, are outside Serbia's control or politically hard.
learnings.quote: Considering the current status of fulfilment of the market coupling preconditions, it is highly unlikely that any Contracting Party will be able to join SDAC and SIDC before 2027. Consequently, CBAM payments are expected to apply from 1 January 2026 to electricity imports from Contracting Parties into the EU.

learnings.title: Serbia cut SO2 sharply yet still breaches Large Combustion Plant ceilings
learnings.programme: Energy Community Large Combustion Plants Directive – National Emission Reduction Plan (NERP)
learnings.problem: Serbia's lignite power plants emit SO2 and NOx above the ceilings that have applied under Energy Community law since 1 January 2018.
learnings.solution: Serbia applies the Large Combustion Plants Directive through a National Emission Reduction Plan with falling emission ceilings, while some units ran under an opt-out regime that expired at the end of 2023.
learnings.implementer: Government of Serbia and thermal power plant operators
delivery_partners: Energy Community Secretariat (monitoring and dispute settlement)
learnings.results: In 2024 Serbia significantly reduced SO2 and kept within its dust ceiling, but SO2 compliance remains out of reach. The opted-out Morava plant and the three Kolubara A3 units were still operating after the opt-out expired.
learnings.serbia_reason: Serbia's own lignite fleet is failing a binding Energy Community obligation. The Secretariat adds that CBAM will further erode generators' revenues, raising doubts about keeping such plants open.
learnings.adapt_needed: Serbia needs a plant-by-plant decision to retrofit or close, taking account of the rising fuel use from pollution controls and of CBAM costs.
learnings.blockers: Retrofits need substantial capital and raise fuel use and CO2 emissions, while coal plants are seen as critical for system adequacy.
learnings.quote: North Macedonia and Serbia reduced their SO 2 emissions—Serbia significantly—yet compliance with the ceilings remains out of reach. Combined with the gradual lowering of the ceilings, this suggests that breaches are likely to become more severe in the coming years.

learnings.title: Serbia's NECP sets 2050 coal exit while adding new lignite unit
learnings.programme: Serbia NECP and Just Transition Plan
learnings.problem: Serbia's power system relies on lignite, and no Contracting Party has written a coal phase-out into domestic law.
learnings.solution: Serbia's adopted NECP plans to cut lignite use by up to 25% by 2030 compared with 2019 and indicates a 2050 coal phase-out. A Just Transition Plan is under consultation.
delivery_partners: Energy Community Secretariat (Policy Guidelines on Just Transition)
learnings.results: The 350 MW Kostolac B3 lignite unit was commissioned at the end of 2024, taking Serbia's lignite capacity to over 4.3 GW. Serbia is not a Powering Past Coal Alliance member, while North Macedonia plans to convert its coal plants by 2027.
learnings.serbia_reason: Serbia's coal exit plan sits inside its Energy Community NECP and just-transition obligations, and the Secretariat cites 2050 as an example of a far-off date. Adding lignite capacity works against the plan's direction.
learnings.adapt_needed: Serbia would need a plant-by-plant closure timetable and a finalised Just Transition Plan instead of a single distant end date.
learnings.blockers: Coal still supplies a large share of electricity and new lignite capacity has just been commissioned, so there is pressure to keep using it.
learnings.quote: However, North Macedonia and Ukraine have included fixed coal phase-out dates in their adopted national planning documents. The Serbian NECP indicates a coal phase-out date of 2050 in the energy mix and the Serbian Just Transition Plan is currently under consultation.

learnings.title: Serbia completes MRVA transposition and issues about 100 GHG permits
learnings.programme: Monitoring, reporting, verification and accreditation (MRVA) of GHG emissions
learnings.problem: Without verified installation-level emissions data, Serbia can neither run a credible carbon price nor show compatibility with the EU framework.
learnings.solution: Serbia transposed the core EU ETS Directive provisions and the EU monitoring, reporting, accreditation and verification rules, and began issuing GHG permits and approving monitoring plans. This obligation is also written into the Western Balkan Reform Agendas.
learnings.funding: Progress on MRVA is a condition for EU support under the Reform and Growth Facility of the Growth Plan for the Western Balkans.
learnings.results: Serbia has completed transposition and approximately 100 GHG permits have been issued. The National Accreditation Body is preparing to review the first applications from verifiers.
learnings.serbia_reason: This is Serbia's own groundwork for a domestic carbon price; the Secretariat calls MRVA the backbone of any emissions trading scheme. EU Growth Plan funding conditions helped drive it.
learnings.adapt_needed: Serbia now needs working accreditation and verified annual emission reports before a carbon tax or ETS can rely on the data.
learnings.blockers: Building the procedural and institutional framework is described as a major challenge for public authorities and operators.
learnings.quote: In Serbia, the transposition process has been completed; entities subject to the new obligations are preparing applications for the approval of GHG permits and monitoring plans and approximately 100 GHG permits have already been issued. The National Accreditation Body is preparing to review the first applications for accreditation submitted by verifiers.

learnings.title: Regulated household tariffs shield consumers but strain public utilities
learnings.programme: Regulated retail electricity prices
learnings.problem: State intervention keeps household electricity prices far below EU levels, so consumers do not see wholesale or CBAM-driven cost changes.
learnings.solution: Serbia and several neighbours have been gradually raising regulated household prices towards market-based supply costs.
learnings.results: Household prices excluding taxes rose 9.29% in Serbia in 2024, yet household prices across the Contracting Parties stayed at about one-third of the EU-27 average. Serbia's industrial prices stayed stable and closer to EU levels.
learnings.serbia_reason: Serbia's retail price shield is paid for mainly by public utilities or the state budget. The Secretariat warns that it delays adaptation to CBAM and to market integration.
learnings.adapt_needed: Serbia would need to keep moving tariffs towards cost, with targeted protection for vulnerable households instead of a general price shield.
learnings.blockers: Raising household electricity prices is politically sensitive.
learnings.quote: As a result, the financial impacts of CBAM-driven changes in cross-border trade are unlikely to be felt directly by these groups. However, this insulation delays or prevents corrective and adaptation measures, increasing vulnerability and placing additional financial strain on the entities providing the price shield—primarily public utilities or state budgets.
